title: The Excel Environment, Tables and Referencing
learning_objective: Navigate the Excel interface (Ribbon, Formula Bar, Name Box, sheet tabs, Status bar), convert a range into a structured table and refer to its columns by name, apply relative and absolute cell references correctly using F4, and identify a cell's underlying data type from its alignment rather than its display format.
description_for_ai: The Ribbon holds every command across its tabs, with context tabs appearing only when something relevant is selected. The Formula Bar shows what a cell actually contains (a formula, number, or text), not what it displays. The Name Box names the selected cell or range and jumps to any address typed into it. Sheet tabs separate one workbook into multiple worksheets; raw data, working calculations, and output belong on separate sheets. The Status bar shows the sum, count, and average of a selected numeric range instantly, with no formula. Every cell has an address built from its column letter and row number (e.g. J2). Useful keystrokes: Ctrl+Home returns to A1; Ctrl+End jumps to the last used cell, revealing how large a file really is; Ctrl+Arrow travels to the edge of a data block (add Shift to select on the way); Ctrl+T converts a selected range into a structured table; F4 cycles a cell reference through its four forms. A structured table (Ctrl+T) knows its own boundaries and expands automatically when rows are added, unlike a plain range (e.g. A2:Q1026) which Excel has no way of recognising the edges of, so formulas built on a fixed range silently exclude new rows. Inside a table, structured references replace cell addresses: [@[Unit price]] means "the Unit price on this row"; TableName[Sales] means "the whole Sales column", and both keep working however many rows the table grows to; a structured reference also survives a new column being inserted, which a fixed address like A2:Q1026 does not. Relative references (e.g. B1) shift when a formula is copied to a new cell; absolute references ($B$1) stay locked on both column and row, which is what a single shared input (a tax rate, a threshold) needs; mixed references (B$1 or $B1) lock only one part. F4, applied to a reference selected inside the Formula Bar, cycles it through B1, $B$1, B$1, $B1, and back to B1; the dollar signs should never be typed by hand. Data type diagnostics: numbers align right by default, text aligns left, and TRUE/FALSE align centre, so a number that is left-aligned is actually stored as text and will not sum. Number formatting is a display facade only: a cell showing a rounded or currency-formatted figure still calculates on its full underlying value, never on what is displayed. Excel's Golden Rule: any formula input that can change (a rate, a threshold) belongs in its own labelled cell, referenced with an absolute reference; only a genuine constant (such as 12 months in a year) is safe to type directly into a formula.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Clicking past the "My table has headers" checkbox when converting a range to a table, producing generic Column1, Column2 headers instead of the real ones. Leaving a shared input such as a tax rate unlocked (using B1 instead of $B$1) so a formula copied down a column walks into empty cells and silently returns zero with no error. Pressing F4 an extra time and locking the row reference too, so the formula stops shifting down a column at all. Building a pivot table or chart on a fixed range instead of a structured table, so new rows are ignored. Leaving a converted table named Table1, Table2, or Table3 instead of renaming it to something that tells the next person what it holds.
example_code_for_ai:
=Subtotal*B1 copied down without locking B1 returns zero on later rows once B2, B3, etc. are empty.
=[@Subtotal] * $B$1   ' correct: the shared rate is locked
=SUM(RawSales[Sales])   ' structured reference sums the whole Sales column regardless of table size
=[@[Unit price]] * [@Quantity]   ' Subtotal calculated per row using structured references

title: Core Formulas and Functions
learning_objective: Choose the correct function family (logical, lookup, text, date, or aggregate) for a stated business question, build the matching formula against a named table (IF/IFS, VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP/INDEX-MATCH, TRIM/LEFT/TEXTSPLIT, TODAY/DATEDIF, SUM/AVERAGE/COUNT/COUNTA/COUNTIF/SUMIF), and verify every result against a figure already known to be correct.
description_for_ai: A logical test is an expression that evaluates to TRUE or FALSE (e.g. [@Rating]>=7); any maths operation turns TRUE into 1 and FALSE into 0, which is why AND behaves like multiplication (one FALSE, i.e. 0, zeroes the whole result) and OR behaves like addition (one TRUE is enough to push the total above zero). IF returns one of two outcomes; once a question has three or more outcomes, IFS takes an ordered list of condition/result pairs, tested in sequence and stopping at the first match, with TRUE as the final catch-all condition; conditions should be ordered strictest to loosest so a loose condition never fires ahead of a stricter one. Lookup family: VLOOKUP(lookup_value, range, column_number, FALSE) searches the first column of a range and returns a value from a numbered column to its right; omitting FALSE performs an approximate match that returns a wrong row without an error, and inserting a column to the left of the answer silently breaks the column count. XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array) names both columns directly, defaults to an exact match, and survives an inserted column, but is missing from older Excel installations. INDEX-MATCH (INDEX(return_range, MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_range, 0))) also names both columns and works in every version of Excel. Text family: TRIM removes leading, trailing and doubled internal spaces; LEN counts characters, so comparing LEN before and after TRIM proves a hidden space exists; LEFT(text, n) pulls a fixed number of characters from the start of a value; TEXTSPLIT(text, delimiter) spills a value across neighbouring cells and returns #SPILL! if its path is blocked; text comparisons ignore case everywhere except inside Power Query, so trimming a stray space matters before case differences even come into play. Date family: Excel stores a date as a serial number, which is why a real date can be subtracted, sorted and filtered by month; a date stored as text cannot, and sits left-aligned rather than right-aligned. TODAY() returns and continually updates to the current date; DATEDIF(start, end, unit) measures the gap between two dates in days, months or years; TEXT(date, "mmmm") extracts a formatted part of a date, such as its month name. Aggregate family: SUM totals a column; AVERAGE means a column and ignores blanks automatically (a blank and a zero are not the same thing); COUNT counts numbers only, COUNTA counts anything non-empty; COUNTIF(range, criteria) counts only the rows matching a condition; SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range) totals only the rows matching a condition; a question naming one condition needs the IF-suffixed version, and a question naming two conditions needs COUNTIFS or SUMIFS. Evaluate Formula (Formula tab, Formula Auditing group) steps through a calculation one operation at a time in the order Excel actually applies it, revealing each intermediate value. Key error codes to read rather than just clear: #VALUE! (a piece of the formula holds the wrong data type), #REF! (a referenced cell has been deleted), #DIV/0! (division by zero or an empty cell), #NAME? (a misspelled function or range name), #SPILL! (a spilled formula's path is blocked by existing data).
common_mistakes_for_ai: Leaving FALSE out of VLOOKUP and getting a silently wrong approximate match instead of an error. Nesting three or four IF statements instead of switching to IFS once there are more than two outcomes. Using SUM or COUNT when the question actually named a condition, where SUMIF or COUNTIF was needed instead. Putting the loosest IFS condition first, so the strictest condition never fires. Assuming multiplication and division run before a reference operator such as the colon in a range. Trusting a formula because it returned a number rather than an error, without checking that number against something already known to be correct.
example_code_for_ai:
=IFS([@Rating]>=8,"Highly Satisfied", [@Rating]>=7,"Satisfied", TRUE,"Needs Follow-up")
=VLOOKUP(F1, RawSales[#All], 2, FALSE)   ' FALSE forces an exact match
=XLOOKUP(F1, RawSales[Invoice ID], RawSales[Branch])
=INDEX(RawSales[Branch], MATCH(F1, RawSales[Invoice ID], 0))
=TRIM([@[Product line]])
=LEN([@[Product line]])            ' 21 before trimming
=LEN(TRIM([@[Product line]]))      ' 18 after trimming, proving 3 invisible characters existed
=SUMIF(RawSales[Branch], "Ikeja", RawSales[Sales])
=COUNTIF(RawSales[Rating], ">=7")

title: Data Cleaning in Excel
learning_objective: Identify and repair the five faces of bad data (duplicates, inconsistent formats, stray spaces, mixed data types, impossible values) in a fixed order (spaces, formats, data types, duplicates, then impossible values), and confirm the cleaned file's row count matches the stated expected total.
description_for_ai: Duplicates are rows representing the same real event, defined by whichever column the business issues once per transaction (e.g. Invoice ID); Remove Duplicates run with every column ticked, the default, only catches exact full-row copies and misses disguised duplicates (the same sale recorded with a different date format, a different case on one field, or a blank left on one of the two rows); running it on the single defining column instead catches every disguised copy too. Inconsistent formats: Excel treats differently-cased text as different values ("Food and beverages" versus "FOOD AND BEVERAGES"), and a text-formatted date will not sort, filter by month, or subtract from another date; PROPER(TRIM(text)) standardises casing, and the order matters: TRIM before PROPER, or a trailing space survives inside an otherwise tidy-looking value; UPPER and LOWER are also available, and Data > Text to Columns with a DMY date setting re-parses a text date into a real one. Stray spaces are invisible on screen and the most common single cause of a lookup returning #N/A or a pivot table silently splitting one category into two rows; TRIM removes leading, trailing and doubled internal spaces, and comparing LEN(text) against LEN(TRIM(text)) turns an invisible problem into a provable number. Mixed data types: a number stored as text will not sum, sort or average correctly, and often carries a small green triangle; ISNUMBER(cell) tests whether Excel will calculate with a value; VALUE(text) converts a text number back into a real number, and DATEVALUE(text) does the same for a text date; ISBLANK(cell) and COUNTBLANK(range) test for and count empty cells. A blank cell is a decision, not an accident: leave it when the blank itself is meaningful (AVERAGE and SUM ignore blanks automatically), flag it with a separate status column when the row is needed but the true value cannot be confirmed, or fill it only when another source confirms the true value; a guessed value is worse than a visible blank. Impossible values (a negative Quantity, a Rating outside its stated scale) differ from outliers, which are merely surprising: an impossible value must be corrected (only when another column proves the true value, e.g. cogs divided by Unit price recovers a true Quantity), flagged, or removed as a last resort once confirmed as an error with no recoverable correct value; every decision should be written down with its reason. Sorting a column smallest to largest is the cheapest way to surface impossible low values at a glance (a mixed column sorts numbers first, then text, then FALSE, then TRUE, then errors, with blanks always last). The fixed cleaning order, stray spaces, then formats, then data types, then duplicates, then impossible values, exists because cleaning the quiet problems first is what makes disguised duplicates visible before they are judged; running the duplicate check before spaces and formats are fixed causes disguised copies to be missed. The row count check: run COUNTA on the column that defines a transaction (e.g. Invoice ID) before and after cleaning; the difference must equal something nameable (e.g. "25 duplicated Invoice IDs, and nothing else"), reconciled against the client's stated expected total; an unexplained drop of even one row means stop, since something was removed that nobody decided to remove.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Deleting an impossible value before checking whether another column can confirm the true one. Running Remove Duplicates with every column left ticked, so disguised duplicates survive. Correcting one cell by hand instead of applying the repair down the whole column. Filling blank cells with a zero so the column "looks complete", when a zero is a rating and a blank is a missing rating. Skipping the row count check because the file looks fine on the surface.
example_code_for_ai:
=PROPER(TRIM([@[Product line]]))   ' TRIM before PROPER, not after
=LEN([@[Product line]])            ' 21
=LEN(TRIM([@[Product line]]))      ' 18, proving 3 invisible characters existed
=ISNUMBER(K2)
=COUNTBLANK(Q:Q)                   ' count of blank Rating cells
=ABS([@Quantity])                  ' compared against cogs / Unit price, to recover a true quantity
=COUNTA(RawSales[Invoice ID])      ' row count check, run before and after cleaning

title: Pivot Tables
learning_objective: Build a pivot table that summarises a verified dataset by one dimension and by several at once (a cross-tab), assign the correct summary calculation deliberately in the Values area rather than accepting Excel's guess, apply filters and slicers and connect one slicer to multiple pivot tables, and verify a pivot total against the source data with an independent formula before sharing it.
description_for_ai: A pivot table has four areas: Rows (what gets one line per category, e.g. one line per branch), Columns (a second dimension spread across the top, turning a list into a cross-tab), Values (the only area that does arithmetic, and the one Excel most often guesses wrong), and Filters (excludes data from the whole pivot, and the most common cause of a pivot that is quietly incomplete when it is shared). Dropping a numeric field into Values defaults to Sum; dropping a field containing any text or blank defaults to Count instead, and a Count appearing where a Sum was expected is a signal that the column holds something non-numeric. Value Field Settings (right-click a value) lets you deliberately choose Sum, Average, Count, Min, or Max, and the resulting default header (e.g. "Sum of Sales") should be renamed to something a reader understands. Dropping a Date field into Rows offers grouping (e.g. by Month), which only works correctly if the underlying values are real dates, not text. Right-click a value, Show Values As, % of Column Total, turns a totals view into a share-of-whole view. A filter dropdown sits in the Filters area, applies to one pivot table only, and its state is easy to leave on by accident; a slicer sits visibly on the sheet as clickable buttons, its state is obvious at a glance across the room, and a single slicer can connect to several pivot tables at once through Report Connections (Ctrl-click selects several items together). Report Layout: a new pivot opens in Compact form, collapsing every field into one unlabelled column; PivotTable Design, Report Layout, Show in Tabular Form names every field again, and File, Options, Data, Edit Default Layout sets this permanently for future pivots. Number formatting must be set on the pivot's value cells themselves; formatting the source column does not carry through. A pivot table never refreshes itself: editing the underlying data leaves the pivot showing the old numbers with no warning until you right-click and Refresh, and a pivot built on a plain range never picks up new rows on refresh, only one built on a structured table does. Verifying a pivot total: rebuild one figure independently with a SUMIF against the source table; if the two agree, the pivot is safe to share; if they disagree, neither figure is trusted until the cause is found, usually a still-active filter, a field placed in the wrong area, or a source that changed after the pivot was built; a mismatch is never resolved by picking whichever number looks preferable.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Building the pivot table from a plain range instead of the structured table, so new rows are silently ignored on refresh. Sharing a pivot table with a filter quietly still applied. Assuming the pivot updates automatically the moment the source data changes. Leaving default headers such as "Sum of Sales" and "Count of Rating" unrenamed. Accepting a pivot total because it looks about right instead of checking it against an independent formula.
example_code_for_ai:
' Verify a pivot total independently:
=SUMIF(CleanSales[Branch], "Trans-Amadi", CleanSales[Sales])
' Should equal the pivot's Trans-Amadi total exactly.
' Value Field Settings: change Count of Rating to Average of Rating
' Right-click a value, Show Values As, % of Column Total

title: Charts and Dashboard Reporting
learning_objective: Choose the correct chart type for a stated question before building anything (a sorted bar chart for "which is biggest", a line chart only for a genuine time sequence, a pie chart only for two or three clearly different shares, a scatter plot for a relationship between two variables), strip Excel's chart defaults and label the result so it needs no explanation, and assemble charts into a one-screen, single-slicer dashboard and test it against the question it was built to answer.
description_for_ai: Chart type follows from the question asked, not from habit. "Which is biggest" calls for a sorted bar chart, because the eye compares bar lengths against a shared baseline better than it compares anything else. "How did it change over time" calls for a line chart, which is legitimate only when the categories have a genuine sequence, such as months, and not for unordered categories such as branches. "What share of the whole" calls for a pie chart only when there are two or three parts that differ obviously; with several similar-sized slices a pie forces the reader to read the labels instead of seeing the answer, so a sorted bar chart is used instead. "How do two things relate" calls for a scatter plot. Chart defaults to delete: the generic "Chart Title" placeholder; a legend on a single-series chart, which names the one thing twice; gridlines sitting behind bars that already carry data labels; 3D effects, shadows and gradients, which distort perceived length; and an extra chart added only because the screen looked empty. What to add instead: a title linked to a cell (click the title, type an equals sign, click the cell, press Enter) so it updates itself and states the finding rather than a generic label; axis labels naming the unit; data labels when the exact figures matter to the decision; one highlight colour on the bar the reader should look at first; and a largest-to-smallest sort applied to every categorical chart. A trend still needs honesty about its denominator: a weaker month's total may simply reflect fewer days or fewer transactions, and that context belongs in the spoken or written narration, not left for the chart alone to imply. A dashboard is a layout decision, not a charting one, and is built by testing against a written question: one dedicated sheet, kept separate from raw data and pivot tables; everything visible on one screen with no scrolling, since scrolling breaks the comparison the dashboard exists to make; the chart that answers the main question placed top-left, where the eye lands first; a single slicer connected to every chart on the sheet through Report Connections, so one click moves the whole screen together; and gridlines turned off (View tab). A dashboard passes when someone can answer the written question from it within a few seconds, using only what is on screen and no further explanation; if it takes longer, the fix is almost always the layout rather than another chart. Charts should always be built from a verified pivot table, never from raw data, so that the chart inherits the reconciliation already carried out on the pivot.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Choosing a pie chart because it looks more finished, on slices of similar size that the reader cannot actually rank at a glance. Leaving the default "Chart Title" in place. Connecting a slicer to some charts on the dashboard but not all of them. Applying conditional formatting to a pivot table including its totals row. Adding a fourth chart because the screen looks empty, instead of fixing the layout. Building a chart from raw data instead of from the verified pivot underneath it.
example_code_for_ai:
' Link a chart title to a cell:
' click the chart title, type =, click the cell, press Enter
' Build a PivotChart from a verified pivot:
' PivotTable Analyze, PivotChart, Bar
' Connect a slicer to multiple charts:
' right-click the slicer, Report Connections, tick every pivot and chart

title: Power Query
learning_objective: Import data into Power Query both from a table already in the workbook and from an external file, add and reorder transformation steps in Applied Steps and explain why the order changes the result, and refresh a query against a new source file, verifying the row count and a few spot values rather than assuming the refresh was correct.
description_for_ai: Power Query automates a cleaning pass so it reruns identically on any file pointed at it, trading manual repetition for repeatability rather than raw speed; the row count verification stays a human job even once the steps themselves are automated. The editor has three zones: the preview grid (centre, shows the result of the steps so far on a sample, and nothing touches the workbook until the query is loaded), Applied Steps (right-hand pane, every action recorded as a named, ordered step that can be renamed, reordered or deleted), and the ribbon (Home, Transform, Add Column, where each button writes a new step). Every manual cleaning action has a query equivalent: Transform, Format, Trim is TRIM applied permanently to a column; Transform, Format, Capitalize Each Word is PROPER; right-click a column, Remove Duplicates, is the same duplicate-defining decision made by hand (choosing one defining column, not every column); Change Type, Date is the query version of Text to Columns. Step order still matters, and is now visible and reorderable: placing Remove Duplicates above Trim in Applied Steps catches only exact copies and returns more rows than expected, because Power Query treats differently-cased text as different values just as a worksheet does; dragging Trim above Remove Duplicates corrects the count. A query can start two ways: From Table/Range, using a table already in the workbook, or From File, using an external file such as next month's export; starting From Table/Range means new rows in that table are picked up automatically. Refresh reruns the same transformations, in the same order, against whatever data now sits at the source; it guarantees that the steps ran, not that the result is correct, since a new export with a renamed column, a new category spelling, or a new date format can break a step silently. After any refresh, the habit is to check the row count and a couple of spot values, not to re-check every value in the file.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Adding steps in whatever order they occur to you and checking only at the end, instead of checking the preview after each step that could change the row count. Deleting a step without checking whether a later step depends on it. Assuming a successful refresh means a correct result. Starting the query from a plain range instead of a table. Treating the query as a black box nobody needs to read, instead of renaming steps so Applied Steps documents the reasoning for a colleague.
example_code_for_ai:
' Applied Steps, correct order:
' 1 Source (From Table/Range)
' 2 Trimmed Text, Product line
' 3 Capitalized, Product line
' 4 Changed Type, Date
' 5 Removed Duplicates, on Invoice ID only
' Wrong order (Remove Duplicates before Trim) returns more rows than the correct order does
' Verify after loading: =COUNTA(Query1[Invoice ID])

title: AI-Augmented Excel
learning_objective: Write a four-part prompt (context, data description, task, output format) to have an AI assistant generate, explain, or debug an Excel formula or Power Query transformation order, verify every AI-produced result against a total already known to be correct before trusting it, and describe what Copilot in Excel changes about that workflow and what it does not change.
description_for_ai: A general-purpose AI assistant cannot see the workbook: it knows a column name, a table name, a value's valid range, or whether a file has been cleaned only if the user types that information in, and it answers confidently anyway when context is missing, filling gaps with a plausible guess that looks identical to real knowledge; it can never know the correct answer, because it cannot open the file. A usable prompt has four parts: context (what the data is, where it lives, what state it is in, e.g. "a cleaned 1,000-row supermarket sales table named CleanSales"), the data description (exact column names and, where relevant, the value range, e.g. "Rating is a number from 4.0 to 10.0 in column Q"), the task (one thing, stated plainly), and the output format (what should come back, e.g. "a single Excel formula using structured references, with no explanation"). Verification workflow: generate the AI's answer for a task already solved by hand earlier in the module, paste it into the workbook, and compare it row for row against the known-correct version (e.g. =SUMPRODUCT(--(yours<>theirs)) should return 0); when debugging, hand the assistant the broken formula plus what was expected and what actually happened, since "it does not work" alone is not enough to diagnose; when asking for an explanation, also ask what happens if a specific input changes, then change that input in the sheet and check the prediction, since a confident explanation and a correct one read identically until tested. A formula can pass verification and still be a poor deliverable: an AI-generated formula that buries a changeable threshold inside itself, rather than referencing a labelled input cell, breaks the Golden Rule from Topic 2.1 even though it returns correct values on every row; verification answers "is it right", not "can the next person maintain it". When an AI-produced figure disagrees with a manually calculated one, the manual figure is trusted and the AI result is investigated; the usual causes are an ambiguous term in the prompt, the wrong column named, or the raw file used instead of the cleaned one. The same verification discipline applies to Power Query logic: describe a transformation in plain English, ask which tools and order to use, compare the suggested order against what was already proven by hand (e.g. trimming must come before deduplicating), then load it and check the row count before trusting a word of it. Copilot in Excel differs from a browser-based assistant in what it can see: it reads the selected data directly from the workbook and needs no column descriptions typed out by hand, and it is licensed and provided by an employer rather than free; it does not remove the need to verify every result exactly as before.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Pasting a generated formula into the real file before testing it. Writing a vague prompt and accepting whatever comes back, instead of supplying all four prompt parts. Trusting a confident explanation without testing its prediction by changing the input. Asking for a figure without stating in the prompt which file, which columns, and which cleaning state applies. Treating a matching answer on one task as proof the assistant understood the problem generally.
example_code_for_ai:
' Compare an AI-generated formula against your own, row for row:
=SUMPRODUCT(--(yours<>theirs))   ' 0 means every row agrees
' Yours (Topic 2.2): =IF([@Rating]>=7,"Satisfied","Needs Follow-up")
' AI's:                =IF(Q2>=7,"Satisfied","Needs Follow-up")
' A correct but unmaintainable AI formula (threshold buried inside):
=IF([@Rating]>=8,"High",IF([@Rating]>=7,"OK","Follow up"))
' Fixed to follow the Golden Rule (threshold in its own labelled cell):
=IFS([@Rating]>=$B$1,"High",[@Rating]>=$B$2,"OK",TRUE,"Follow up")
